stories.title: AI Turns the Entire Bible Into More Than 30,000 Songs
stories.summary: A 28-year-old Nashville entrepreneur used AI to turn every single verse of the Bible into music — over 30,000 songs across 11 genres in English and three in Spanish. It started when his pastor dad asked for one chapter set to music for a sermon.
stories.extended_summary: What started as a favor for his pastor father — set 1 John 4 to music for a sermon illustration — became 30,000 songs. Micah Fiechter's app Music Bible uses AI to turn every verse of Scripture into music without changing a single word, instead reshaping the music to fit the text. There's hip-hop, pop, country, children's music, 11 genres in English and three in Spanish, with more languages planned. The goal isn't catchy worship hits — it's helping people actually remember what they're hearing.

stories.title: Seattle software engineer turned general contractor built an AI guide to the patchwork of permit rules
stories.summary: Seattle software engineer Pascal Matta built a free AI tool to decode the confusing patchwork of municipal permit rules after struggling with his own deck project. The site covers 457 verified rules across 80 jurisdictions, saving homeowners from endless PDFs and guesswork.
stories.extended_summary: Pascal Matta has a background building software for tech giants like Google and T-Mobile. But when he wanted to have a deck added to his Seattle home, he discovered that municipal code was far trickier than software code. After trying to sort through a mess of permitting regulations for a deck he never had built, Matta decided to tackle the problem himself in two ways. First, he started Kolmo Construction, his own Seattle-based general contracting company. Second, he built a free online tool to decipher convoluted permit rules in the city and elsewhere. The site, kolmo.io/permits, serves as an un-gated database designed to answer the questions that usually send homeowners into a spiral of municipal PDFs. The AI-powered tool covers 457 verified rules across 80 jurisdictions in King, Pierce, and Snohomish counties, linking each rule directly to specific city source pages and exact wording rather than forcing users to rely on rough guesses and Google searches. 'It exists because the information genuinely isn't anywhere else,' Matta says.

stories.title: At 16, Parker Fawcett Is Building Software—and Testing the Limits of AI Coding Agents
stories.summary: At just 16, Parker Fawcett is already an AI engineer at CHG Healthcare, building an ed-tech startup, and researching how AI coding agents actually build software. His open-source project Rebuild Dossier tackles a tricky question: if an AI passes its tests, how do you really know the code works?
stories.extended_summary: Most 16-year-olds are stressing about homework. Parker Fawcett is working as an AI engineer at one of the largest healthcare staffing companies in the US, running his own ed-tech startup, and doing original research on how AI coding agents build software. It started when he noticed AI models generating working code while quietly leaving behind dead code and junk endpoints. Instead of asking the AI to clean up after itself, he extracted the app's expected behavior and rebuilt it from scratch in a separate environment. That experiment became Rebuild Dossier, an open-source project now chasing a deceptively hard question: if an AI coding agent passes its tests, how do you actually know the software is sound?
